prompt: Deliver a eulogy for a deer stand. You may not mention death, the deer stand itself, or any form of the word 'hunt' — and every listener must still know exactly what is being mourned.
response:
# A Eulogy

Friends, we gather at the base of this old oak to say goodbye.

For twenty-three autumns, she held us. Fifteen feet up, wedged in the crook where the trunk splits, she was our seat above the world. Every October, before the sun thought about rising, one of us would climb her weathered rungs — quietly, always quietly — settle onto her plywood floor, lean a rifle against her rail, and wait.

And oh, how she taught us to wait.

She taught us that the forest wakes in layers: first the squirrels, then the crows, then — if we were patient, if we were still — the soft crunch of hooves in frost-covered leaves. From her height, we watched whitetails move like ghosts through the November gray. Some mornings we filled our tags. Most mornings we filled only our thermoses, twice. She never judged either outcome.

She held three generations. Grandpa built her from scrap lumber and stubbornness in 1987. Dad reinforced her railings the year I turned twelve, the year I first climbed up beside him in the dark, my breath fogging, my heart pounding louder than the woods. Last season, I lifted my own daughter onto that same platform and watched her eyes go wide at a ten-pointer stepping into the clearing below.

But winters are cruel to wood, and this spring we found her leaning, her boards soft with rot, her ladder no longer to be trusted. Some things cannot be repaired — only remembered.

So we take her down with gratitude. We'll salvage a plank or two for the mantel. We'll build again in the same tree, because the tree still stands and the whitetails still come.

She asked nothing of us but silence and patience. She gave us sunrises, stories, and one another.

Rest easy, old girl. The woods won't be the same without you in them.
